questions.stem: A pancreatic cell secretes large amounts of a digestive enzyme. Which set of organelles is most directly required to make and export that protein?
options: Nucleolus, peroxisomes, and smooth ER
Smooth ER, mitochondria, and lysosomes
Rough ER, Golgi apparatus, and transport vesicles
Ribosomes, lysosomes, and the cytoskeleton
questions.why: Secretory proteins are built on ribosomes bound to the rough ER, processed and sorted in the Golgi, then carried to the membrane in vesicles.

questions.stem: An essay argues that students no longer use the school library and offers a 2014 district survey as its only support. Which change would most strengthen the argument?
options: Add recent circulation counts and door tallies for the past three years
Quote a retired librarian who remembers busier afternoons
Repeat the 2014 figure in the conclusion for emphasis
Note that the survey was conducted by the district itself
questions.why: The claim is about present behavior, so current usage data speaks to it directly; a memory and a repeated statistic add no new support.

questions.stem: A leaf is supplied with carbon dioxide labeled with radioactive carbon and kept in bright light. In which molecule does the label first appear as a stable product of the Calvin cycle?
options: Ribulose bisphosphate, which accepts the incoming carbon
Glucose, which is the pathway's final product
Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, formed after reduction
3-phosphoglycerate, formed as the carbon is fixed
questions.why: Rubisco attaches the carbon to RuBP, and the unstable six-carbon intermediate splits at once into two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate.

questions.stem: A student writes: "The district should ban phones in class. After all, every teacher I interviewed supports a ban." Which statement best describes the weakness in the support?
options: It mistakes correlation for causation between phones and grades
It rests on a sample too small and too self-selected to generalize
It assumes the very conclusion it sets out to prove
It appeals to emotion instead of offering any reason
questions.why: Interviewing teachers the writer chose produces a tiny, biased group, so it cannot show what the staff as a whole think.

questions.stem: A hormone receptor activates a G protein that turns on adenylyl cyclase. A mutation locks the G protein in its GTP-bound state. What is the most likely effect when hormone is added?
options: cAMP rises even without fresh hormone, so the response stays on
cAMP falls, because adenylyl cyclase can no longer be reached
The receptor stops binding hormone, which ends the signal
The response is unchanged, because G proteins relay only once
questions.why: A GTP-locked G protein cannot switch itself off, so adenylyl cyclase keeps producing cAMP and the pathway is stuck active.

questions.stem: In a speech on school funding a principal says: "We are not asking for luxuries. We are asking for paper. We are asking for heat." The short repeated fragments chiefly serve to
options: establish the speaker's technical expertise in budget policy
concede that the district has mismanaged its money
make an ordinary need feel urgent and hard to refuse
steer the audience toward a different proposal
questions.why: The bare, repeated fragments stack concrete needs, which builds urgency while framing the request as minimal rather than extravagant.

questions.stem: A cell produces a DNA polymerase that lacks proofreading activity. Which outcome is most likely when this cell copies its genome?
options: Replication halts completely, so no new DNA is made
Mismatched bases persist more often, raising the mutation rate
The sugar-phosphate backbone dissolves and copying stops
Chromosomes fail to condense when mitosis begins
questions.why: Proofreading removes mispaired bases just after they are added, so without it replication proceeds but more errors survive into the daughter strands.

questions.stem: A writer cites a study reporting that students who eat breakfast earn higher grades, then concludes that schools should serve breakfast. Which evidence would most strengthen that conclusion?
options: A survey showing that most students enjoy breakfast food
An estimate of what a breakfast program would cost
A nutritionist's explanation of a balanced diet
A trial in which schools added breakfast and grades rose
questions.why: The original finding is only correlational; an intervention in which breakfast was added and grades then improved is what supports a causal claim.

questions.stem: A repressor protein sits on an operator site and blocks transcription of an operon. A sugar enters the cell and binds that repressor. What happens next?
options: RNA polymerase binds the promoter more tightly
The operon's genes are deleted from the chromosome
The repressor leaves the DNA, so transcription can start
Translation of the messenger RNA already made stops
questions.why: Binding the sugar changes the repressor's shape so it releases the operator, which frees RNA polymerase to transcribe the operon.

questions.stem: An editorial argues: "Our graduation rate rose after we added a study hall, so the study hall caused the rise." Which unstated assumption does that reasoning depend on?
options: No other change in that period could explain the increase
Graduation rate is the best single measure of a school
Students assigned to study hall wanted to graduate
The study hall was popular with the faculty who ran it
questions.why: Moving from sequence to cause requires assuming nothing else changed; without that, another reform could account for the higher rate.

questions.stem: Beetles of one species live on dark soil and light soil. Over many generations dark beetles become common on the dark soil and light beetles on the light soil. Which process best explains this pattern?
options: Genetic drift acting alone in a very large population
Selection favoring beetles that match their background
Gene flow carrying dark alleles in from a distant site
Mutation creating dark alleles only where soil is dark
questions.why: Predators remove beetles that stand out, so each soil type selects for the color that hides its carriers — selection, not drift or mutation.

questions.stem: An essay on a factory town describes the river this way: "It ran orange past the school, and the children swam in it anyway." The sentence chiefly works by
options: citing water-quality figures for the region
praising the town's tradition of outdoor recreation
explaining the chemistry behind the discoloration
letting an image carry a criticism the writer never states
questions.why: The flat report of orange water and swimmers implies negligence without accusing anyone, so the image does the arguing.

questions.stem: Two species share a recent common ancestor and both have a trait that a third, more distantly related species lacks. On a cladogram that shared trait is best read as
options: a shared derived character inherited from that ancestor
an analogous feature that evolved twice on its own
an ancestral trait that says nothing about relationship
proof that all three species are equally related
questions.why: A trait inherited from a recent common ancestor is a shared derived character, and those are what define a clade.

questions.stem: A student wants to cite a blog post that summarizes a peer-reviewed study the student has not read. What is the strongest move for the essay?
options: Cite the blog and note that many people share it online
Cite the study and quote the blogger's summary as its finding
Read the study, cite it directly, and state what it cannot show
Drop the evidence and rely on personal experience instead
questions.why: Citing the primary source after reading it keeps the claim accurate and lets the writer name the study's limits rather than borrowing them secondhand.

questions.stem: A person is infected for the first time with a virus. Which response appears earliest and is least specific to that particular virus?
options: Antibody release by plasma cells derived from activated B cells
Formation of memory T cells that persist after recovery
Clonal expansion of helper T cells that recognize one antigen
Inflammation and phagocytosis by macrophages at the site
questions.why: Innate responses such as inflammation and macrophage engulfment act within hours and without regard to which pathogen is present.

questions.stem: A draft reads: "Later start times improve attendance. Any parent who disagrees is simply out of touch." Which revision best strengthens the argument for a school board audience?
options: Keep the claim and add a sharper adjective about parents
Concede the scheduling costs, then answer them with attendance data
Cut the attendance claim and describe the writer's own mornings
Add that most students also dislike early alarms
questions.why: Conceding a real cost and answering it shows the writer weighed objections, which persuades a skeptical board better than dismissing parents.

questions.stem: During an action potential, voltage-gated sodium channels open and then quickly inactivate. What does that inactivation accomplish?
options: It keeps sodium entering so the signal can travel farther
It prevents reopening, so the impulse moves in one direction
It opens potassium channels before sodium ever enters
It restores the resting potential by pumping sodium out
questions.why: Inactivated channels cannot reopen until the membrane repolarizes, which creates the refractory period and keeps the impulse one-way.

questions.stem: A column about a school board meeting begins: "The board met for three hours, and the agenda survived." The tone of that sentence is best described as
options: dryly ironic, suggesting little was accomplished
openly furious about the board's decisions
warmly nostalgic about earlier meetings
strictly neutral, passing no judgment at all
questions.why: Saying the agenda 'survived' treats the meeting as an ordeal to be endured, which signals quiet mockery rather than plain reporting.

questions.stem: On a hot, dry afternoon a plant closes its stomata. Which immediate effect best explains why water uptake by the roots slows?
options: Root pressure reverses direction and pushes water upward
Phloem loading stops, so sugar no longer moves downward
Transpiration pull weakens, lowering tension in the xylem
Xylem walls thicken and physically block the water column
questions.why: Water rises mainly under tension created by transpiration, so closing stomata cuts the pull and slows movement up the column.

questions.stem: An opponent of a later start time says: "Either we keep the current schedule or we abandon academics entirely." The statement is most vulnerable because it
options: attacks the character of the people proposing the change
rests on a single anecdote about one late student
assumes that schedules cause student achievement
offers only two options where others plainly exist
questions.why: The sentence forces a false choice; a modified schedule is an available middle option that its framing excludes.

questions.stem: A kelp forest loses most of its sea otters to disease. Urchin populations then explode and strip the kelp. Which term best describes the otter's role in that community?
options: Keystone species, whose removal restructures the community
Primary producer, supplying energy to the food web
Invasive species, introduced from another region
Dominant competitor that excludes urchins by resource use
questions.why: The otter's removal cascades through the whole community, which is the defining effect of a keystone species.

questions.stem: A pamphlet reports that "87 percent of students surveyed said the new schedule helped them." Before citing it, a writer should most importantly ask
options: whether the students enjoyed filling out the survey
how the students were selected and how many responded
whether the pamphlet was printed in color
how long the new schedule has been in place
questions.why: A percentage means little without the sample size and selection method; a small or self-selected group can easily produce a misleading 87 percent.

questions.stem: An enzyme loses all activity when heated to 75 °C and regains none of it after cooling. Which explanation best fits that result?
options: Its peptide bonds were broken into free amino acids
The substrate was denatured along with the enzyme
Its folded shape was disrupted, distorting the active site
Its cofactors were consumed during the reaction
questions.why: Heat breaks the weak bonds holding the tertiary fold; once the active site's geometry is lost for good, cooling cannot restore it.

questions.stem: The same writer argues for a later start time in a research paper and in a two-minute public comment at a board meeting. Which difference matters most in adapting the argument?
options: The paper needs more metaphors than the spoken comment
The comment should include the whole literature review
The paper should address students rather than adults
The comment must land one claim quickly, without citations
questions.why: A short spoken comment cannot carry footnotes and extended reasoning, so the claim and its single best piece of evidence must be compressed.

questions.stem: Nondisjunction occurs in meiosis II of one human cell. If both of the abnormal gametes it produces are fertilized by normal sperm, what chromosome counts result?
options: Both zygotes carry the usual 46 chromosomes
One zygote has 44 and the other has 48
One zygote has 45 and the other has 47
Both zygotes carry 47 chromosomes
questions.why: Meiosis II nondisjunction gives one gamete an extra chromatid and the other one too few, so those zygotes end up at 47 and 45.

questions.stem: A proposal opens with a budget table listing a $40,000 auditorium upgrade, then describes a classroom where students share torn textbooks. The juxtaposition chiefly works to
options: show that the auditorium project is legally improper
make the district's priorities look misplaced without arguing it
show that the writer supports both expenditures equally
summarize district spending in a carefully neutral way
questions.why: Setting the spending beside the shortage invites readers to draw the judgment themselves, which persuades more than stating it outright.

questions.stem: Two true-breeding white-flowered strains are crossed and all the F1 plants have purple flowers. The F2 generation shows a 9:7 ratio of purple to white. Which explanation fits?
options: Two genes act in one pathway, and both dominant alleles are needed
One gene shows incomplete dominance, giving three phenotypes
The trait is sex-linked and expressed in only one sex
A single gene carries a recessive allele that is lethal
questions.why: A 9:7 ratio is the 9:3:3:1 dihybrid pattern with the three minor classes pooled, the signature of complementary genes in a single pathway.

questions.stem: A student's draft thesis reads: "School uniforms are a topic that many people have opinions about." Which revision turns it into an arguable claim?
options: School uniforms have been worn in many countries for decades.
Some students like uniforms, and some students dislike them.
Uniforms come up at many school board meetings each year.
Uniform rules can cut morning conflict, but only if students help choose them.
questions.why: Only the fourth option makes a specific, contestable claim with a condition a reader could dispute; the rest report that opinions exist.

questions.stem: A diploid cell with 2n = 6 completes meiosis. Which statement about the gametes it produces is correct?
options: Each gamete carries six chromosomes, half of them maternal
Each gamete carries three chromosomes in one of several combinations
Each gamete carries three chromosomes, all from the same parent
Each gamete carries twelve chromosomes after replication
questions.why: Meiosis halves the diploid number to three, and independent assortment of the three pairs yields several possible maternal-paternal mixes.

questions.stem: A survey asks: "Do you agree that the district wastes money on unnecessary programs?" A writer cites the 71 percent agreement as proof of waste. The strongest objection is that the question
options: was asked of too few administrators to matter
produced a percentage that cannot be averaged
builds its conclusion into the wording, so agreement proves little
should have been translated into other languages
questions.why: The question assumes waste already exists, so agreeing with it is not evidence that waste exists — a leading question manufactures its own result.

questions.stem: A PCR product is run on a gel beside a size ladder. The sample shows a single band that sits between the 500 and 600 base-pair markers. What has been established?
options: The sample holds no DNA, since only one band appeared
The DNA was cut into many fragments of varied sizes
The product is longer than every fragment in the ladder
A product of roughly 550 base pairs is present in the sample
questions.why: Migration distance tracks fragment length, so a band between two ladder sizes indicates a product of about the size between them.

questions.stem: A writer revises "The team lost, and the season ended, and everyone went home" to "The team lost. The season ended. Everyone went home." The revision chiefly
options: breaks the events into separate beats, giving each one weight
adds causal links among the three events described
makes the passage more conversational and less formal
clarifies which event the writer thinks mattered most
questions.why: Splitting the clauses into short sentences spaces the events out so each lands on its own instead of blurring into one chain.

questions.stem: A tumor suppressor gene is inactivated in one cell, and that cell begins dividing without the usual checks. Which best explains how the loss contributes to cancer?
options: It speeds up repair of damaged DNA in that cell
It converts the cell into one that produces gametes
It removes a brake on the cycle, so damaged cells keep dividing
It raises the rate of apoptosis in nearby tissue
questions.why: Tumor suppressors normally halt the cycle until damage is repaired; losing one removes that brake and lets mutations accumulate.

questions.stem: During prophase I, each pair of homologous chromosomes comes together along its length and forms a structure of four chromatids. What is that structure, and what happens inside it?
options: A tetrad; sister chromatids separate at the centromere.
A tetrad; non-sister chromatids exchange segments at chiasmata.
A bivalent; homologous chromosomes move to opposite poles.
A synaptonemal complex; the chromosomes replicate a second time.
questions.why: Synapsis holds the homologs together as a tetrad of four chromatids, and crossing over at chiasmata swaps segments between non-sister chromatids. Homologs separate later, in anaphase I.

questions.stem: An essay argues: "Earlier school start times give students more time for extracurriculars, so they are better for students." Which revision makes the thesis most defensible?
options: Earlier start times are obviously the best choice for every district in the country.
Earlier start times are better for students, and anyone who disagrees is uninformed.
School start times have been debated for many years in many different places.
Earlier start times may expand afternoon options, but districts should weigh that gain against adolescent sleep needs.
questions.why: A defensible thesis makes a specific claim and concedes the strongest objection. The first option overreaches, the second attacks opponents instead of arguing, and the third asserts nothing.

questions.stem: A karyotype is made by photographing a cell's chromosomes, cutting them out, and arranging them into pairs. Why must the cells be sampled at metaphase rather than at interphase?
options: At metaphase the chromosomes are condensed and individually distinguishable.
At metaphase each chromosome has completed a second round of replication.
At metaphase the homologs have already separated into different cells.
At metaphase crossing over is finished, so the two chromosomes of a pair are identical.
questions.why: Karyotyping needs condensed, visible chromosomes; interphase chromatin is diffuse and cannot be sorted by size. Homolog separation is anaphase I, and crossing over makes the pair non-identical, not identical.

questions.stem: A student argues that the district should fund after-school tutoring. Which evidence would most strengthen that claim?
options: A survey in which students say they like the idea of tutoring.
A national report on the history of after-school programs.
District data showing that students who attended tutoring gained an average of eleven points.
A teacher's statement that tutoring is clearly the right thing to do.
questions.why: Evidence that links the proposed program to the outcome being claimed — measured gains for attendees — carries the argument. Liking the idea, program history and assertion supply no such link.

questions.stem: A karyotype shows 47 chromosomes, including two X chromosomes and one Y. How many autosomes does this cell contain, and what most likely produced the extra chromosome?
options: 45 autosomes; nondisjunction during meiosis II of the father.
44 autosomes; nondisjunction of a sex chromosome in one parent's meiosis.
44 autosomes; crossing over between the X and the Y in prophase I.
47 autosomes; fertilization of one egg by two sperm.
questions.why: 47 total minus three sex chromosomes leaves 44 autosomes. An extra chromosome comes from nondisjunction — failure of homologs or sister chromatids to separate — not from crossing over, which changes alleles rather than chromosome number.

questions.stem: A writer states: "One might object that the policy costs too much. That objection has merit — but it prices the policy against a budget that already absorbs the cost of doing nothing." What does the concession accomplish?
options: It abandons the writer's position in favor of the opposition's.
It shifts the essay's subject from cost to budgeting procedure.
It weakens the argument by admitting a flaw the writer cannot answer.
It grants the objection's force, then reframes the comparison so the objection loses its force.
questions.why: Conceding before reframing builds credibility and controls the terms of comparison. The writer neither gives up the claim nor changes the subject; the concession is a move, not a surrender.

questions.stem: Nondisjunction of chromosome 7 occurs in one secondary spermatocyte during meiosis II. What is the chromosome 7 content of the four resulting sperm?
options: Two normal, one with an extra copy, and one missing a copy.
All four abnormal: two with an extra copy and two missing one.
One with an extra copy and three normal.
All four normal, because meiosis II only separates sister chromatids.
questions.why: Only one of the two cells entering meiosis II divides badly, so half of its products carry the error. Four abnormal products would mean the failure happened in meiosis I instead.

questions.stem: A paragraph builds one long sentence cataloguing a school's failures, then ends: "The roof leaks." What does the short sentence chiefly accomplish?
options: It introduces a new topic the long sentence did not cover.
It signals that the writer has run out of examples.
It isolates one concrete detail so it lands with weight the list could not give it.
It shifts the essay from description into direct address.
questions.why: The abrupt shortening after a cumulative list throws emphasis onto a single concrete detail; the effect depends on the contrast in length, not on new content or a change of audience.

questions.stem: A tall pea plant is crossed with a short plant, and all 60 offspring are tall. What can be concluded about the tall parent, and why?
options: It is heterozygous, because half the offspring would be short if it were homozygous.
It is homozygous dominant, because a heterozygote in that cross would give roughly equal tall and short offspring.
It is homozygous recessive, because no short offspring appeared.
Nothing can be concluded, because 60 offspring is too few to reveal a 1:1 ratio.
questions.why: Crossing to the recessive parent exposes a hidden allele: a heterozygote yields about 1:1, and the complete absence of short offspring in 60 tries indicates no recessive allele is present.

questions.stem: An op-ed begins: "In 1954, this city closed its public pools rather than integrate them." The next paragraph turns to a current vote on a community center. What does the opening chiefly do?
options: It supplies statistical evidence for the argument that follows.
It establishes the author's personal connection to the issue.
It concedes that the current proposal has a troubled history.
It frames the present decision as a recurrence of a familiar local choice.
questions.why: The historical anecdote works as a frame, setting up the current vote as another instance of the same choice and shaping how the reader judges it. It offers no data, no personal claim and no concession.

questions.stem: An organism has a diploid number of 12. Assuming independent assortment and no crossing over, how many genetically different combinations of chromosomes can its gametes carry?
questions.why: With 2n = 12 the haploid number is 6, and each of six pairs orients independently, giving 2 to the sixth, or 64. Using 12 as the exponent double-counts by treating the diploid number as n.

questions.stem: An education essay summarizes district reading scores, then quotes a mother describing her son hiding his textbook from classmates. What does the quotation add to the paragraph's argument?
options: It substitutes an anecdote for the data, weakening the claim.
It supplies the policy recommendation the data lack.
It converts an abstract number into a human cost the reader can feel.
It shows that the data were collected improperly.
questions.why: The quotation particularizes the statistic, giving the number a face without disputing it. The data still carry the claim; the anecdote supplies pathos and concreteness.

questions.stem: Two genes lie far apart on the same chromosome. In one meiosis a crossover occurs between them. What is the result for the gametes of that meiosis?
options: The two genes now assort independently, so four gamete types appear in equal numbers.
Gametes carry new combinations of alleles for the two genes, not only the parental combinations.
The chromosome number in each gamete increases by one.
The two genes are deleted from the recombinant chromatids.
questions.why: Crossing over exchanges segments between non-sister chromatids, producing recombinant chromosomes with allele combinations the parent did not have. It changes which alleles travel together, never the chromosome count.

questions.stem: A writer claims the school should keep its late-start schedule. Which sentence best refutes the counterclaim that later starts conflict with sports practice?
options: Sports are enjoyable for many students, but academics matter too.
Anyone who puts practice before sleep has their priorities wrong.
Many schools have sports programs of various kinds.
Districts that moved practice to the morning kept both schedules, and their teams' participation did not fall.
questions.why: The strongest refutation meets the objection's actual mechanism — practice timing — with evidence that both goals were met. The other three dismiss, insult or sidestep the claim.

questions.stem: At a locus in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 42 percent of the population is heterozygous and the recessive allele is the rarer of the two. What is q?
questions.why: Heterozygotes are 2pq = 0.42, so pq = 0.21. With p + q = 1, q(1-q) = 0.21 gives q = 0.3 or 0.7; because q is the rarer allele, q = 0.3 and p = 0.7.

questions.stem: A report says a company "harvested" user data and "mined" its customers' messages. What does this diction imply about the company's relationship to its users?
options: That the company treated users as partners in a shared project.
That the company was legally barred from using the data.
That users were a resource to be extracted rather than people served.
That the company's methods were agricultural and therefore outdated.
questions.why: Harvest and mine construe people and their messages as raw material to be taken, carrying an exploitative charge the neutral word collected would not.

questions.stem: If cohesin at the centromeres is not cleaved during meiosis II, what is the direct consequence for that division?
options: Homologs fail to separate in meiosis I, producing two n+1 and two n-1 gametes.
Sister chromatids stay joined, so the products end up with the wrong chromosome number.
Crossing over cannot occur, so no recombinant chromosomes form.
The chromosomes replicate again before the division can finish.
questions.why: Centromeric cohesin holds sister chromatids together; without its cleavage at anaphase II they cannot separate. Arm cohesin cleavage is the meiosis I event, and crossing over belongs to prophase I.

questions.stem: A draft argues for a later school start in four paragraphs and mentions the bus-schedule objection only in its final sentence. What revision would most improve the argument?
options: Delete the objection, since raising it weakens the case.
Move the objection into the title so readers see it first.
Add three more paragraphs of supporting statistics before the objection.
Address the objection in its own paragraph before the conclusion, then answer it.
questions.why: A serious objection buried in a closing sentence reads as an afterthought. Answering it mid-essay both concedes its weight and lets the writer rebut it before the reader leaves.

questions.stem: Meiosis and fertilization alternate in a sexual life cycle. What does that alternation accomplish for a species?
options: It keeps the chromosome number of each generation from doubling.
It ensures that every offspring is genetically identical to its parent.
It allows gametes to divide again before fertilization.
It replaces mutation as the source of new alleles.
questions.why: Meiosis halves the chromosome number and fertilization restores it, so the total stays constant across generations. The cycle produces variation; it does not produce clones or new alleles, and gametes do not divide again.

questions.stem: A columnist writes: "My neighbor's daughter was bored in calculus, which proves that the math curriculum fails students." Which flaw is most precisely named?
options: Circular reasoning, because the conclusion restates the premise.
Ad hominem, because the columnist attacks teachers.
Hasty generalization, because one student's experience is offered as proof about a whole curriculum.
False dilemma, because only two options are presented.
questions.why: A single case is generalized into a claim about an entire curriculum, and one student cannot carry that weight. Nothing in the sentence attacks a person, assumes its conclusion, or forces a two-way choice.

questions.stem: Two pea plants heterozygous at two independently assorting loci (AaBb) are crossed. What fraction of the offspring is expected to show the dominant phenotype for A and the recessive phenotype for b?
questions.why: Each locus behaves independently: 3/4 show the dominant A phenotype and 1/4 show the recessive b phenotype, and 3/4 times 1/4 is 3/16. 9/16 is both dominants and 1/16 is both recessives.

questions.stem: Two sources disagree about whether a later start improved attendance: a district report finds a two-point gain, and a state audit finds no change. How should a synthesis essay handle them?
options: Use the district report and omit the audit, since the essay's claim needs support.
Use the audit and call the district report biased without saying why.
Report both and let the reader decide, without comment.
Compare their methods and time frames, then explain which finding the claim can rely on.
questions.why: Synthesis means weighing sources rather than selecting convenient ones. The disagreement is itself evidence, and explaining it through method differences shows the reasoning a strong essay is graded on.

questions.stem: A population of 40 lizards is isolated on a small island. Over five generations its allele frequencies shift sharply even though every genotype survives equally. Which Hardy-Weinberg condition does this population most clearly fail?
options: A large population; in a small population, chance sampling error changes allele frequencies.
No mutation; drift cannot occur unless new alleles appear each generation.
Random mating; drift occurs only when mates are chosen by phenotype.
No selection; equal survival normally guarantees stable allele frequencies.
questions.why: Genetic drift is sampling error, and its effect grows as population size falls. Equal survival rules out selection, and drift needs neither new alleles nor assortative mating.

questions.stem: A speech asks: "If we cannot afford to fund the library now, when exactly will we be able to?" What does the rhetorical question accomplish?
options: It requests specific budget figures that the speaker intends to supply.
It concedes that funding may never be possible.
It assumes an answer — never — that the audience is invited to accept as obvious.
It shifts the entire decision to the audience without making an argument.
questions.why: The question is not seeking information; it frames delay as permanent so the audience supplies the devastating answer itself, which persuades more effectively than stating it outright.

questions.stem: In a human male's karyotype the X and Y chromosomes are placed as a pair. In what sense are they a homologous pair?
options: They carry identical genes, so they are fully homologous.
They synapse and segregate during meiosis even though they differ in size and gene content.
They are autosomes that happen to differ in shape.
They are homologous only because both were inherited from the mother.
questions.why: Sex chromosomes behave as a pair in meiosis — they synapse and separate like homologs — although they differ in length and carry different genes. Only a small region of the Y matches the X.

questions.stem: A student editorial argues for a later start time but addresses "the school board" throughout, citing budget line items and district policy. Which revision best fits publication in the school newspaper?
options: Add more budget line items so the argument is fully documented.
Address the board more formally and use additional policy terminology.
Remove all evidence, since students do not care about facts.
Recast the claim around students' own experience and what they can ask the board to do.
questions.why: Audience determines which evidence and appeals are usable. Student readers need their own stake named and an action they can take, while budget detail aimed at the board reads as irrelevant to them.

questions.stem: Meiosis has one S phase but two divisions. What would follow if a cell replicated its chromosomes between meiosis I and meiosis II?
options: Each gamete would carry twice the DNA it should, undoing the reduction meiosis exists to produce.
Crossing over would occur a second time, doubling the variation.
Homologs would re-pair and rebuild the tetrads.
Nothing would change, because the second division would separate the extra copies.
questions.why: The point of two divisions after a single replication is to halve both chromosome number and DNA content. A second S phase would restore diploid DNA in every product.

questions.stem: A letter argues: "My opponent wants to cancel all sports so students can study more." The opponent's actual proposal adds one study hall each week. Which flaw is present?
options: Hasty generalization from a single example.
Circular reasoning that assumes the conclusion.
Straw man: the opponent's position is restated in an extreme form that is easier to attack.
Appeal to authority that substitutes prestige for evidence.
questions.why: The letter replaces the real proposal with a caricature — cancel all sports — and then refutes the caricature. That is a straw man, not an inference drawn from too little evidence.

questions.stem: A student writes: "Crossing over is how new alleles are created." Which correction is most accurate?
options: Crossing over creates new alleles whenever it occurs between non-sister chromatids.
Crossing over produces new combinations of alleles that already exist; only mutation creates new alleles.
Crossing over creates new alleles, but only during meiosis II.
Crossing over creates new alleles only in species that have many chromosomes.
questions.why: Recombination shuffles alleles that already exist, which is where most of a generation's variation comes from; the alleles themselves originate as mutations.

questions.stem: A board member defends a policy: "The new grading policy is fair, because it treats every student fairly." Which flaw is most precisely named?
options: False dilemma: only two options are considered.
Post hoc: sequence in time is treated as cause.
Ad hominem: critics are attacked instead of answered.
Circular reasoning: the conclusion is offered as its own justification.
questions.why: No independent reason is given — fair is simply asserted again in different words, so the sentence cannot support its own claim.

questions.stem: A plant cell is placed in a solution whose solute concentration is higher than the cell's. Which prediction about water movement and the cell's response is correct?
options: Water leaves the cell by osmosis, and the protoplast shrinks away from the cell wall.
Water enters the cell, and turgor pressure rises.
Water moves equally in both directions, so the cell does not change.
Solutes move into the cell until concentrations match, so no water moves.
questions.why: Water moves toward the higher solute concentration, so a hypertonic bath pulls water out; in a plant cell the membrane then pulls away from the wall, which is plasmolysis.

questions.stem: An essay about a city's housing shortage ends: "So who exactly is the plan for?" What does closing on this question accomplish?
options: It restates the thesis in simpler language.
It introduces a new argument the essay never developed.
It leaves the reader to supply the damning answer the essay's evidence has made unavoidable.
It withdraws the essay's claim and leaves the issue open.
questions.why: The closing question delivers the essay's claim in the reader's own voice: the evidence has already pointed to an answer, and asking the question transfers the judgment to the reader.

questions.stem: A single nucleotide is deleted near the beginning of a coding sequence, and the resulting protein is nonfunctional. Which explanation best accounts for the effect?
options: The deletion removed the start codon, so translation never began at all.
The deletion shifted the reading frame, so every downstream codon was misread and the protein's sequence changed.
The deletion changed one codon, substituting a single amino acid for another.
The deletion added a stop codon at the same position, leaving the protein unchanged.
questions.why: A one-nucleotide deletion shifts the reading frame from that point onward, altering every downstream codon and usually producing an early stop — far more damaging than a single substitution.

questions.stem: A student measures reaction rate as substrate concentration rises. The rate climbs, then levels off, and adding more enzyme raises the plateau. Which best explains the plateau?
options: The reaction has reached equilibrium, so forward and reverse rates are equal and net product stops changing.
All active sites are saturated, so the rate is limited by the number of enzyme molecules rather than by substrate concentration.
The substrate has been entirely converted to product, so no further reaction can occur.
The enzyme denatures at high substrate concentration, permanently ending catalysis.
questions.why: The plateau is saturation: at high substrate concentration every active site is occupied, so the rate is capped by enzyme amount. That is why adding enzyme raises the plateau.

questions.stem: An editorial states: "Screens are almost certainly a factor in the decline, though the evidence so far is correlational, and the decline began before smartphones were widespread." The writer's qualifications chiefly serve to
options: build credibility by naming the limits of the evidence while still advancing the claim
concede that the claim is unsupported and should be withdrawn
shift blame from screens onto smartphones
signal that the writer has no position on the issue
questions.why: Naming the correlational limit and the timeline keeps the claim standing while showing the writer has weighed the evidence, which is what earns trust with a skeptical reader.

questions.stem: Isolated mitochondria are supplied with pyruvate and oxygen while a drug blocks the electron transport chain. Which immediate consequence best explains why ATP synthesis stops?
options: Pyruvate can no longer be oxidized to acetyl-CoA, so the citric acid cycle receives no carbon.
Cytosolic glycolysis halts because ATP synthase is the cell's only source of ATP.
Protons are no longer pumped into the intermembrane space, so the gradient driving ATP synthase collapses.
Oxygen binds ATP synthase directly and prevents phosphorylation of ADP.
questions.why: ATP synthase is a turbine run by the proton gradient. Blocking electron transport stops proton pumping, the gradient dissipates, and phosphorylation halts even though substrate is present.

questions.stem: A proposal opens with two captions: "The 1998 gym, before. The 2026 gym, after: same square footage, twice the students." It then argues for a new facility. The side-by-side captions chiefly
options: establish the writer's expertise in facilities planning
concede that the building has been well maintained
shift the argument from students to budgets
make the strain visible without the writer asserting it directly
questions.why: The juxtaposition lets the reader infer the crowding from the two facts, so the argument's premise arrives as an observation rather than as a claim the writer must defend.

questions.stem: A plant is given CO2 labeled with a heavy isotope under continuous light. In which molecule does the label first appear, and why?
options: In 3-phosphoglycerate, because rubisco fixes CO2 onto RuBP in the Calvin cycle.
In glucose, because the light reactions assemble sugar directly from CO2.
In oxygen, because CO2 is split at photosystem II.
In ATP, because the label enters the proton gradient before being fixed.
questions.why: Carbon fixation is the first step that incorporates CO2: rubisco attaches it to RuBP, and the unstable six-carbon product splits immediately into two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate.

questions.stem: A student's essay opens by conceding that standardized tests predict first-year grades, then never mentions testing again while arguing for portfolio assessment. The chief problem with this concession is that it is
options: placed too early, which weakens the writer's ethos with a skeptical audience
dropped rather than answered, so it sits beside the argument instead of advancing it
insufficient, since one concession cannot satisfy opponents of the proposal
irrelevant, since first-year grades have nothing to do with assessment policy
questions.why: A concession earns its place only when the writer turns it — granting a point and then showing why the argument survives it. Left unanswered, it reads as an unrelated admission.

questions.stem: In a cell, DNA polymerase works normally but DNA ligase is nonfunctional. Replication opens the fork and then stalls on one new strand. Which best explains the stall?
options: Helicase cannot unwind the double helix without ligase, so the fork never opens.
Primase cannot lay down RNA primers, so synthesis never begins.
Topoisomerase cannot relieve supercoiling, so the fork reverses.
Okazaki fragments are synthesized but cannot be joined, leaving unsealed nicks in the lagging strand.
questions.why: Ligase seals the nicks between Okazaki fragments. Without it the lagging strand accumulates unjoined fragments, while the continuously synthesized leading strand is largely unaffected.

questions.stem: An op-ed on school funding is written by a retired principal of thirty years in that district, and it opens: "I have sat in the meetings where these budgets were cut." The opening chiefly
options: establishes that the writer has read the budget documents
appeals to emotion by describing the length of the writer's career
grounds the writer's authority in direct experience of the specific decisions at issue
suggests that only career educators can evaluate a budget
questions.why: The claim to authority is narrow and specific — presence at those meetings — which is more persuasive than a general appeal to thirty years of service.

questions.stem: A mutation prevents the G1/S cyclin from being degraded. Which outcome is most likely, and why?
options: Cells pass the G1 checkpoint without the usual requirement for growth signals, favoring continued division.
Cells arrest in G2 permanently, because cyclin degradation is required for mitosis to begin.
Cells replicate their DNA twice per cycle, because S phase re-fires immediately after finishing.
Cells never enter mitosis, because cyclin must be destroyed to activate CDKs.
questions.why: Cyclin levels rise and fall to gate each transition; a cyclin that cannot be cleared keeps its CDK active, so the G1/S brake is released without the normal growth-signal requirement.

questions.stem: Defending a phone ban, a writer argues: "A hallway without a phone policy is a highway without lane markings — everyone is capable, and nobody is safe." The main weakness of the analogy is that it
options: compares places of very different size, so the comparison is factually inaccurate
relies on the audience's fear of accidents instead of evidence about learning
concedes that students are capable, which undercuts the case for a ban
assumes hallway order comes from a posted rule, which is the very point the argument needs to prove
questions.why: The analogy borrows the highway's case for markings and applies it to hallways, where order may come from supervision, schedules, or norms — so it assumes rather than supports the ban.

questions.stem: Researchers replace a membrane's unsaturated fatty acid tails with saturated ones and hold the temperature at 37 degrees C. What happens to fluidity, and why?
options: Fluidity rises, because saturated tails pack loosely and leave gaps.
Fluidity falls, because saturated tails pack more tightly and raise the temperature needed for the same fluidity.
Fluidity is unchanged, because cholesterol alone sets membrane fluidity.
Fluidity first rises and then falls, because saturated tails melt and then crystallize.
questions.why: Saturated tails lack the kinks that keep unsaturated tails apart, so they pack closely and stiffen the bilayer; the membrane needs a higher temperature to reach its previous fluidity.

questions.stem: An administrator's memo says a failing program will be "sunset" and that the affected families will be "transitioned to other options." The diction most likely
options: softens an ending by replacing plain terms with ones that sound procedural and inevitable
signals that the program's end is temporary and will be reviewed
shows that the administrator does not know which families are affected
appeals to families' emotions in order to win their support for the change
questions.why: "Sunset" and "transitioned" borrow the neutrality of a process, which removes the sense that anyone decided to end the program or that families are losing something.

questions.stem: A ligand binds a receptor tyrosine kinase whose kinase domain is inactive. Which step is blocked first, and why?
options: The ligand cannot bind the receptor, so no signal is received.
G proteins cannot exchange GDP for GTP at the receptor.
Receptor autophosphorylation fails, so adaptor proteins have no docking sites to recruit.
Second messengers cannot be degraded, so the signal never terminates.
questions.why: After dimerization the receptor phosphorylates itself, and those phosphotyrosines are what adaptor proteins bind. No kinase activity means no docking sites and no relay downstream.

questions.stem: After describing a flooded basement, mold in three classrooms, and a collapsed ceiling tile, a reporter writes: "The building has some maintenance needs." The understatement chiefly
options: shows that the reporter has not verified the extent of the damage
offers the district's perspective to balance the earlier details
signals that the damage is less serious than the paragraph suggested
lets the gap between the evidence and the wording carry the criticism
questions.why: The reader has just seen the list, so the mild phrasing lands as dry judgment: the writer never says the district is negligent, and does not have to.

questions.stem: An insect population is sprayed for ten generations. Resistance rises sharply and allele frequencies shift. Which statement best explains the shift?
options: The insecticide caused resistant mutations in individual insects, which then passed them to offspring.
Pre-existing resistant variants survived and reproduced more, so their alleles rose in frequency.
The insects learned to break down the insecticide and passed the learned trait to their offspring.
Gene flow from untreated populations introduced resistance alleles in every generation.
questions.why: Selection changes frequencies in a standing pool of variation; the mutations were already present at low frequency, and the spray removed the insects that lacked them.

questions.stem: A district newsletter praising its new "paperless initiative" arrives as a four-page color mailer to every household. The situation is ironic chiefly because
options: the format of the announcement contradicts the change it announces
the district spent money on printing during a budget crisis
households did not request the newsletter
the initiative is described as new when paperless systems are long established
questions.why: The irony is structural: the channel contradicts the message, since the claim to have gone paperless is printed on four pages of paper.

questions.stem: A cell has solute potential -0.6 MPa and pressure potential 0.2 MPa. It sits in a beaker whose solution has a water potential of -0.5 MPa. What is the direction of net water movement?
options: Out of the cell, because its solute potential is more negative than the solution's.
No net movement, because pressure potential cancels solute potential.
Into the cell, because the cell's water potential of -0.4 MPa is higher than the solution's -0.5 MPa.
Out of the cell, because pressure potential adds to the solute potential and lowers the total.
questions.why: Water potential is solute plus pressure: -0.6 + 0.2 = -0.4 MPa inside. Water moves from higher water potential (-0.4) toward lower (-0.5), so it enters the cell.

questions.stem: A student writes, "Reading scores fell six points (District Report 2025). This proves the curriculum failed," while the report itself attributes the fall to a new test format. The best revision is to
options: drop the citation, since the report contradicts the claim it is used to support
add a second citation that agrees with the claim so the evidence is balanced
keep the claim and note that the report's explanation is only one interpretation
report what the source actually says, including its explanation, and narrow the claim to what it supports
questions.why: Citing a source while suppressing its explanation misrepresents it. Honest integration states the finding and the caveat, then claims only what survives the caveat.

questions.stem: Two species share a trait their recent ancestors lacked, and the trait arises from different genes in each lineage. How should a phylogeneticist treat this trait?
options: As an analogous trait produced by convergent evolution, so it should not define a clade.
As a homologous trait inherited from a shared ancestor, so it does define a clade.
As a derived trait useful for rooting the tree at that node.
As an ancestral trait too widespread to be informative about relationships.
questions.why: Similar function built on different genes means independent origin. Grouping by that trait would create a false clade, which is why cladistics relies on shared derived homology.

questions.stem: A conclusion reads: "The district should fund tutors, extend library hours, and it should also be training teachers in reading instruction." The most useful revision chiefly
options: shortens the sentence so that each item receives equal emphasis
makes the three recommendations grammatically parallel so they read as one coordinated proposal
puts teacher training first, since it matters most
adds a fourth recommendation to show the scale of the problem
questions.why: The third item breaks the pattern with a new subject and verb, so it drops out of the list. Matching the form keeps all three inside a single, unified recommendation.

questions.stem: A storm reduces a fish population from 500 to 12 survivors. In the next generation an allele that had been rare is now common. Which best explains this?
options: Selection favored the allele during the storm, so the survivors were the fittest fish.
Mutation rates rose after the storm and produced the allele repeatedly.
The bottleneck sampled only a few alleles by chance, so drift shifted frequencies independently of fitness.
Gene flow from a larger population introduced the allele after the storm.
questions.why: A population crash leaves a random handful of alleles in the survivors. That is the bottleneck effect: frequency change from sampling, not from the allele being better suited to the habitat.

questions.stem: An essay argues schools should teach "media literacy" and spends its first body paragraph defining the term through three practices: tracing a claim to its source, following a statistic to its study, and reading a headline against its article. Defining the term this way chiefly
options: fixes a contested term to specific practices, so later claims can be evaluated
shows that media literacy is already taught in some schools
appeals to the audience's distrust of headlines
narrows the essay's audience to teachers who already agree
questions.why: A vague label invites agreement from everyone and commitment from no one. Defining it by practices converts it into something the argument can then show is missing or teachable.

questions.stem: In a bacterium, a repressor binds the operator only when a co-repressor is bound to it, and the structural genes are transcribed whenever the co-repressor is absent. What kind of control is this?
options: Positive control, because the co-repressor activates transcription of the operon
Inducible control, because transcription switches on when a substrate appears
Catabolite repression, because the available carbon source sets the transcription rate
Repressible negative control, because the repressor blocks transcription unless the co-repressor is absent
questions.why: The default state is on and the regulatory protein turns it off, so the control is negative; the product of the pathway activates the repressor, which is the signature of a repressible operon.

questions.stem: A college essay about a summer warehouse job is built from short declaratives and includes the line "I learned the difference between tired and unable." The style chiefly
options: demonstrates that the writer knows warehouse work from the inside
lets restraint carry the meaning, so the lesson arrives without being announced
shows that the writer is not yet ready for academic prose
creates suspense about whether the writer kept the job
questions.why: The clipped sentences withhold commentary, which makes the single reflective line do the work; the writer shows the lesson through pacing instead of stating it outright.

questions.stem: Fragments of 200, 800, and 2,000 base pairs are loaded into an agarose gel and electrophoresed. Which describes their final positions, and why?
options: The 2,000 bp fragment travels farthest, because it carries more net negative charge.
All three travel equally far, because their charge-to-mass ratios are equal and the gel cannot resolve size.
The 200 bp fragment travels farthest, because smaller fragments pass through the gel matrix more easily.
The 200 bp fragment travels least, because it binds more dye and becomes heavier.
questions.why: Agarose acts as a sieve: all fragments have nearly the same charge per unit mass, so the separating variable is length, and the shortest fragment moves fastest through the pores.

questions.stem: One paragraph ends "Costs rose 12 percent." The next begins "Meanwhile, enrollment fell." The transition is a poor choice chiefly because it
options: signals simultaneous time rather than the contrast or consequence the argument needs
is too informal for an academic essay
repeats the previous paragraph's point instead of advancing it
implies that the two trends cannot be compared
questions.why: "Meanwhile" marks two things happening at once. If the argument's point is that rising costs made falling enrollment worse, the transition hides the relationship the reader needs named.

questions.stem: After an infection a person carries antibody against the pathogen, and a second exposure triggers a faster, larger antibody response. Which cells account for this, and how?
options: Cytotoxic T cells, which retain antibody and release it on re-exposure
Helper T cells, which multiply and secrete antibody directly
Neutrophils, which remember the pathogen's surface and respond faster
Memory B cells, which survive and differentiate rapidly into antibody-secreting plasma cells
questions.why: The secondary response comes from long-lived memory B cells selected in the first infection: they are already present in higher numbers and need fewer signals to become plasma cells.

questions.stem: A column proposes that because students learn best when comfortable, schools should replace desks with beds and exams with naps. The proposal is satirical chiefly because it
options: cites no research on classroom furniture
extends a premise to an absurd conclusion in order to expose the premise's weakness
criticizes students for wanting to be comfortable
recommends a change the writer actually supports
questions.why: Satire follows a claim past the point where its advocates would go. The absurd extension makes the original premise look unexamined without the writer having to argue against it directly.

questions.stem: A tRNA's anticodon mutates so that it pairs with a stop codon, but the tRNA still carries its original amino acid. What is the most likely effect on translation?
options: Translation terminates earlier, because stop codons are recognized sooner.
The mRNA is degraded, because the ribosome detects the anticodon mismatch.
Translation reads past the normal stop and adds an amino acid, because the mutant tRNA competes with release factors.
The amino acid is left uncharged, so the protein comes out one residue shorter.
questions.why: A stop codon ends translation only because no tRNA answers it and a release factor binds instead. A tRNA that answers it inserts an amino acid, so the ribosome keeps going.

questions.stem: An argument states: "If we allow phones during passing periods, then we must allow them during class, and soon we will have no rules at all." The reasoning fails chiefly because it
options: treats a limited allowance as the first link in an inevitable chain without showing the chain is inevitable
compares passing periods with class time without explaining the comparison
offers no evidence about how phones affect learning
addresses an audience that does not actually set policy
questions.why: Each step is asserted, not argued: nothing shows that allowing phones in hallways requires allowing them in class. Without that link the conclusion does not follow from the premise.

questions.stem: A trophic pyramid shows 10,000 kcal at the producer level and about 1,000 kcal at the primary consumer level. Which best explains the loss?
options: Energy is destroyed as it moves up a trophic level, since consumers cannot use all of it.
Producers store only about 10 percent of the sunlight they absorb, so the rest never enters the food chain.
Primary consumers convert most ingested energy into new biomass, so the pyramid should widen upward.
Most energy leaves as heat from respiration and as undigested material, so roughly a tenth is built into consumer biomass.
questions.why: The ten percent rule reflects respiration losses and material that is not assimilated. Energy is not destroyed — it is converted to heat — so less remains to be passed on at each level.

questions.stem: A report finds that students who take four years of math are three times more likely to finish college. An editorial prints this as evidence that requiring four years of math will raise completion rates. The use is weakest because it
options: assumes the statistic is inaccurate without checking the study
converts a correlation among students who chose math into a claim about what a requirement would cause
fails to say which colleges the surveyed students attended
treats a threefold difference as too small to justify a policy
questions.why: Students who elect four years of math differ from those who do not in ways the statistic cannot separate. Turning that group difference into a predicted effect of a mandate is the leap.

questions.stem: On a hot, dry, windy afternoon a plant closes its stomata. Which immediate effect on water movement and photosynthesis is most likely?
options: Transpiration rises, because closing stomata concentrates water vapor inside the leaf.
Xylem tension falls and water uptake increases, because the pull from the leaves stops.
Transpiration falls and CO2 uptake drops, so the Calvin cycle slows for lack of carbon.
Root pressure alone maintains transpiration, so photosynthesis is unaffected.
questions.why: Stomata are both the exit for water vapor and the entrance for CO2. Closing them conserves water but starves the Calvin cycle of carbon, which is why photosynthesis drops at midday.

questions.stem: A spermatocyte from a species with 2n = 8 completes meiosis. Which statement correctly describes the chromosome number in the resulting cells at each stage?
options: Two cells with 4 chromosomes each after meiosis I, then four cells with 4 chromosomes each after meiosis II.
Two cells with 8 chromosomes each after meiosis I, then four cells with 4 chromosomes each after meiosis II.
Four cells with 2 chromosomes each, because replication reduces the chromosome number twice.
Two cells with 4 chromosomes each after meiosis I, then four cells with 2 chromosomes each after meiosis II.
questions.why: Meiosis I separates homologous pairs, halving 2n = 8 to n = 4 per cell; meiosis II separates sister chromatids, so chromosome number stays 4 while DNA content halves.

questions.stem: A student writes: "Online instruction is ineffective (Johnson 2019), and a district survey found that 62 percent of teachers preferred in-person classes." Which statement best identifies the weakness of the second piece of evidence?
options: It is unusable because a survey of teachers is never a legitimate source in an academic argument.
It reports what teachers prefer, which does not establish whether online instruction works.
It lacks a parenthetical citation, so readers cannot verify the number.
It contradicts the Johnson study, and an argument cannot cite conflicting sources.
questions.why: Preference is not a measure of effectiveness, so the second sentence does not support the claim even though it is accurately reported.

questions.stem: In a dihybrid cross of AaBb x AaBb with the two genes on different chromosomes, what fraction of the offspring is expected to show both recessive traits?
questions.why: Each gene independently gives 1/4 homozygous recessive, and independent assortment multiplies the probabilities: 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16.

questions.stem: An essay argues that because the school's recycling program collected less material last year, participation is declining. Which unstated assumption does the argument depend on?
options: That recycling is a worthwhile activity for a school to sponsor.
That the decline was concentrated among this year's senior class.
That the school has enough bins placed around the building.
That the amount collected reflects participation rather than a change in what can be recycled or how collection is measured.
questions.why: The leap from less material to fewer participants only holds if the measurement itself did not change; that is the missing warrant.

questions.stem: Two genes lie 40 map units apart on the same chromosome and are followed in a testcross. What proportion of the offspring is expected to be recombinant?
options: 40 percent
20 percent
10 percent
80 percent
questions.why: Map units equal recombination frequency, so a 40 map unit distance predicts 40 percent recombinant offspring, which is the ceiling before double crossovers make the distance unreliable.

questions.stem: An essay claims that a new cafeteria schedule reduced crowding. Which evidence most directly supports that claim?
options: A survey found that students reported liking the new schedule better than the old one.
Average wait time in the lunch line fell from nine minutes to four after the schedule changed.
The number of students responding to the school's climate survey rose by 200.
Two neighboring districts adopted similar lunch schedules the same year.
questions.why: Wait time is the quantity the claim is about, so a measured drop supports crowding directly rather than by proxy.

questions.stem: Two unaffected parents have a child with a recessive disorder. Their unaffected daughter marries an unrelated unaffected man, and carriers of the allele occur in 1 in 50 people in that population. What is the probability that their first child is affected?
options: About 1 in 200
About 1 in 4
About 1 in 300
About 1 in 150
questions.why: The daughter is a carrier with probability 2/3 given that she is unaffected; multiplied by the partner's 1/50 carrier chance and the 1/4 chance of two carriers having an affected child, the result is about 1/300.

questions.stem: A writer concludes: "Because two studies found a correlation between sleep and grades, schools must start later." Which revision most strengthens the argument?
options: Delete the studies and argue instead from the writer's own experience of being tired in class.
Add an anecdote about one student who improved after sleeping more.
Broaden the claim so that it covers every school schedule in the country.
Narrow the claim to what correlational evidence supports and name the specific students and outcomes it would affect.
questions.why: The original overreaches from correlation to a mandate, so limiting the claim to what the studies show removes the weakest link.

questions.stem: A drug allows microtubules to attach to kinetochores but blocks tension across them. Treated cells arrest in metaphase. Which best explains the arrest?
options: The spindle assembly checkpoint stays unsatisfied without tension, so activation of the anaphase-promoting complex is delayed.
DNA damage detected at the kinetochore halts the cell before S phase can be completed.
Cyclin B accumulates because cytokinesis cannot begin without attached microtubules.
The cell cannot duplicate its centrosome, so the spindle never forms a bipolar array.
questions.why: The checkpoint monitors attachment and tension; without tension the signal that triggers APC activation and separase release never arrives, so anaphase does not start.

questions.stem: A writer on school funding describes "a chemistry lab with fume hoods that vent into the same room students sit in, and a teacher who has learned to teach around the smell." The description chiefly serves to
options: establish the writer's technical credentials in laboratory safety.
make an abstract budget figure concrete and urgent for readers who have never been in the building.
concede that the district has spent money on science facilities.
mock the district administration for incompetence.
questions.why: The sensory detail converts a budget number into a felt cost, which is what moves readers with no direct experience of the school.

questions.stem: In a population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 9 percent of individuals express a recessive trait. What proportion of the population is expected to be carriers?
questions.why: q squared = 0.09 gives q = 0.3 and p = 0.7, so heterozygotes are 2pq = 2(0.7)(0.3) = 0.42; 0.30 is q itself, the recessive allele frequency.

questions.stem: An op-ed cites a think tank's report that the district spends "above average" per student. Before using the figure, a writer should most importantly ask
options: whether the think tank's staff have been quoted in national news coverage.
how many pages the full report runs and whether it includes an appendix.
whether the same figure appeared in the district's own press release.
how the think tank defines and adjusts per-student spending, since the comparison depends on that measure.
questions.why: "Above average" is meaningless until the measure is specified: excluding capital costs, special education, or pension obligations can reverse the comparison.

questions.stem: A color-blind man and a woman who is a carrier of the same X-linked allele have children. Which statement about their offspring is correct?
options: Half the daughters are expected to be color-blind and half carriers, and half the sons are expected to be color-blind.
All daughters will be color-blind, because they inherit an affected X from their father.
All sons will be color-blind, because the allele passes from mother to son.
No daughters can be affected, because the trait is recessive and the mother is only a carrier.
questions.why: Each daughter receives the father's affected X plus either maternal X, and each son receives the mother's X at a 50 percent chance, so both sexes show roughly a 1:1 split for their respective outcomes.

questions.stem: A student arguing for later start times writes: "Critics say later starts would disrupt athletics, but districts that shifted their bus schedules report little conflict." The sentence chiefly
options: abandons the original claim in favor of a narrower one about buses.
concedes an objection and answers it with evidence, which strengthens the claim it is defending.
introduces a second argument that the essay never develops.
appeals to authority without offering any supporting evidence.
questions.why: Naming the strongest objection and rebutting it with evidence is refutation, and it makes the surrounding case harder to dismiss.

questions.stem: A girl with Turner syndrome (45, X) is found to have inherited her single X chromosome from her mother. Which parental event best explains this?
options: Nondisjunction in the mother's meiosis I produced an egg with two X chromosomes.
Nondisjunction in the mother's meiosis II produced an egg with two identical X chromosomes.
Nondisjunction in the father's meiosis produced a sperm lacking a sex chromosome.
A mitotic error after fertilization eliminated one X chromosome from the embryo.
questions.why: If her only X came from her mother, the paternal gamete must have carried no sex chromosome, which points to nondisjunction on the father's side.

questions.stem: A report states that "students who attended the college fair were twice as likely to apply to a four-year school." A writer presents this as proof that the fair causes applications. The strongest objection is that
options: the report did not survey every student in the district.
fair attendance may have fallen in the years after the report.
correlational findings can never inform any school policy.
students already inclined toward college may be the ones who chose to attend the fair.
questions.why: Self-selection means the comparison groups differ before the fair, so the difference in application rates cannot be credited to the fair.

questions.stem: A mutation destroys the 3' splice site at the end of intron 2 in a gene. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Intron 2 is retained in the mature mRNA, shifting the reading frame downstream of the exon 2 boundary.
Intron 2 is translated in its normal frame, leaving the protein unchanged.
Exon 2 is removed from the mRNA along with the intron.
The primary transcript is exported and translated without any splicing at all.
questions.why: Without a recognized 3' site the spliceosome cannot cut there, so the intron stays in the message and any ribosome reading it will frame-shift after exon 2.

questions.stem: A column argues: "Our principal cut the arts budget, and this year's test scores dropped, so cutting the arts lowered scores." The reasoning is most vulnerable because it
options: attacks the principal's motives instead of the decision itself.
treats two events in sequence as cause and effect without ruling out other explanations.
relies on an undefined technical term that readers cannot interpret.
assumes the audience already supports arts funding.
questions.why: Post hoc reasoning: a budget cut followed by a score drop does not show the cut produced the drop, since staffing, test format, or cohort could explain it.

questions.stem: A quantitative PCR assay reports a very low Ct value for a sample. What does this indicate about the sample?
options: The sample contained very little target, so more cycles were needed to reach threshold.
The primers formed dimers, which suppresses amplification of the target.
The target sequence was abundant, so threshold fluorescence was reached after few cycles.
The template was degraded, so amplification started later than expected.
questions.why: Ct is the cycle at which signal crosses threshold; fewer cycles means more starting template, so a low Ct signals high target abundance.

questions.stem: An essay on a city's flood response is written mostly in long, clause-heavy sentences, but one paragraph switches to three short ones: "The water rose. The sirens never sounded. Nobody came." The shift chiefly
options: signals that the writer is uncertain about the facts being reported.
parodies the official style of the city's emergency notices.
marks the essay's turn to a counterargument about preparedness.
slows the reader at the moment of failure and makes the absence of response feel stark.
questions.why: Syntax is doing the work here: stripped, end-stopped sentences isolate each fact so the failure lands one beat at a time.

questions.stem: A skeletal muscle cell is deprived of oxygen during sprinting. Which pair of changes best explains its ATP yield?
options: Glycolysis continues with NAD+ regenerated by lactate formation, so net yield falls to about two ATP per glucose.
The electron transport chain keeps running on stored oxygen, so yield stays near thirty ATP per glucose.
The Krebs cycle accelerates to compensate, producing ATP directly from pyruvate.
Glycolysis stops entirely because pyruvate cannot enter the mitochondrion.
questions.why: Without oxygen as the final electron acceptor, NADH cannot be reoxidized by the chain, so fermentation regenerates NAD+ and only substrate-level phosphorylation remains.

questions.stem: Two studies measure the same tutoring program: a district report finds large gains, and a university study finds none. Which approach best strengthens an argument about the program?
options: Cite only the district report, because local evidence is always more relevant than outside research.
Compare the two designs, including duration, control group, and outcome measure, and argue from what the stronger design supports.
Average the two results and report a moderate improvement.
Note that the sources disagree and decline to recommend anything.
questions.why: The disagreement is information about method, and identifying which design better supports a causal claim is what makes the conclusion defensible.

questions.stem: An inhibitor is added to an enzyme assay. Vmax is unchanged, but Km increases. Which describes the inhibition and its remedy?
options: Noncompetitive inhibition; raising substrate concentration restores the maximum rate by displacing the inhibitor from an allosteric site.
Uncompetitive inhibition; the inhibitor binds only the enzyme-substrate complex and lowers Km.
Competitive inhibition; raising substrate concentration restores the maximum rate because the inhibitor competes for the active site.
Irreversible inhibition; the enzyme is permanently inactivated and no amount of substrate helps.
questions.why: A substrate-displaceable inhibitor that leaves Vmax intact is competitive, so more substrate outcompetes it; noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax instead.

questions.stem: An opinion piece on later start times opens: "I know parents are tired of schedules being rewritten. I am one." The opening chiefly
options: concedes the argument outright and leaves the writer's claim abandoned.
establishes the writer's expert knowledge of adolescent sleep science.
signals an ironic tone toward parents who oppose the change.
establishes shared ground with skeptical readers before the argument asks anything of them.
questions.why: The sentence acknowledges the audience's legitimate fatigue and places the writer inside that group, which earns a hearing for the proposal that follows.

questions.stem: A cell keeps cytosolic Na+ low, and glucose enters against its gradient through a Na+/glucose symporter. What powers the uptake?
options: The Na+ electrochemical gradient, established by the Na+/K+ pump hydrolyzing ATP, drives the symporter.
Direct ATP hydrolysis by the symporter at its cytosolic face.
Facilitated diffusion of glucose through a channel that flips between conformations.
The glucose gradient itself, since the symporter moves both molecules down their gradients.
questions.why: Secondary active transport couples glucose movement to Na+ moving down the gradient the pump paid for; the symporter itself never hydrolyzes ATP.

questions.stem: A writer on school safety quotes a researcher who studied 200 schools, then adds: "That does not settle the question; it only means we have reason to look." The move chiefly
options: undercuts the writer's own case by admitting the evidence is irrelevant.
uses expert evidence while limiting what it can prove, which makes the claim more credible.
shifts the burden of proof onto readers who have not done research.
replaces statistical evidence with an emotional appeal about children.
questions.why: Bounding a claim to its evidence is a deliberate ethos move: the writer keeps authority without overclaiming what one study establishes.

questions.stem: A patient's blood calcium falls well below normal. Which response best restores homeostasis?
options: Calcitonin is secreted, increasing calcium deposition in bone.
Insulin is secreted, driving calcium into skeletal muscle with glucose.
Parathyroid hormone is secreted, raising osteoclast activity and renal calcium reabsorption.
Aldosterone is secreted, increasing calcium reabsorption in the collecting duct.
questions.why: Low blood calcium triggers PTH, which mobilizes bone calcium and reclaims it at the kidney; calcitonin does the opposite and responds to high calcium.

questions.stem: A student's essay on campus safety rests entirely on two anecdotes from classmates. The most useful revision is to
options: remove both anecdotes and rely only on statistics from the district website.
